````math
and list the time of prefilling and decoding for a single trajectory in
Table [7](#A1.T7 "Table 7 ‣ A.2 Additional Results ‣ Appendix A More Experimental Results and Discussion ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning").
Our reward calculation only involves the prefilling stage, which is
significantly faster than the decoding process. This makes our approach
more efficient compared to other self-rewarding methods that generate
both evaluation criteria and final rewards.

#### A.3 Discussion

Q1: Why our methods have the potential to outperform rule-based RL?

First, rule-based RL methods do not assess the quality of the reasoning
process. This poses a risk that incorrect reasoning paths may
coincidentally lead to correct answers and thus receive undeserved high
rewards. Secondly, we evaluate the correctness using intermediate
reasoning states. In contrast, we place greater emphasis on the quality
of the reasoning process rather than the final answer, which leads to
more consistent improvements in reasoning ability.

Q2: How does the method handle universally incorrect samples during RL?

Our reward mechanism may assign zero advantage to completely wrong
answers due to the low consistency of intermediate reasoning states,
which avoids misleading updates. This contrasts with majority voting,
which amplifies dominant errors.

### Appendix B Proof and Analysis

#### B.1 Technical Setting and Notations

Large Language Models. For a prompt $`x\in\mathcal{X}`$, LLMs generate
output distributions in an autoregressive manner, which can be
formulated as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{\theta}(y|x)=\prod_{i=1}^{|y|}\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}|x,y_{<i})=\prod_{i=1}^{|y|}\text{softmax}(f_{\theta}(x,y_{<i})),
``` |  | (13) |

where $`f_{\theta}`$ is a neural network that maps the sequence of
tokens to the logits of the next token, and $`y_{<l}`$ denotes the
prefix of the output sequence up to position $`l-1`$. This
parameterization corresponds to large-scale language models (e.g.,
Transformers) used in practice. However, the non-concavity of the RL
objective poses significant challenges for theoretical
analysis \[[32](#bib.bib32), [1](#bib.bib1)\]. To simplify, existing
studies \[[32](#bib.bib32), [26](#bib.bib26), [1](#bib.bib1)\] often
consider a tabular policy that assigns an independent, trainable logit
to each possible output $`y`$. The tabular policy can be regarded as a
special case of the autoregressive policy, where the output distribution
is directly parameterized, thus facilitating gradient analysis.

Reinforcement Learning Object. Let $`\mathcal{V}`$ be a finite
vocabulary of tokens. We use $`\pi_{\theta}`$ to denote a language
model, parameterized by $`\theta`$, that receives a prompt
$`x\in\mathcal{X}`$ and produces a distribution over outputs
$`y\in\mathcal{Y}`$, where
$`\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathcal{V}^{*}`$ are the sets of
possible input prompts and outputs, respectively. Following convention
in the RL literature, we also refer to $`\pi_{\theta}`$ as a policy. For
a prompt $`x\in\mathcal{X}`$ and reward function
$`r:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\in\{0,1\}`$, we denote the RL objective
for a single prompt $`x\in\mathcal{X}`$ by:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\theta;x)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[r(x,y)\right].
``` |  | (14) |

Optimization. We follow the settings in [Razin et al.
\[32\]](#bib.bib32) and also adopt the gradient flow approximation of
the policy gradient method, assuming an relatively small learning rate.
The resulting dynamical system is described by:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{d}{dt}\theta(t)=\nabla\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\theta(t)),\ \ \ t\geq 0,
``` |  | (15) |

where $`\theta(t)`$ denotes the parameters of the policy at timestep
$`t`$ during training and $`\theta(0)`$ is $`\theta_{\text{ref}}`$. The
gradient flow formulation facilitates the analysis of the optimization
dynamics by eliminating the stochastic noise inherent in gradient-based
updates.

Notations. We use $`\mathbf{e}_{i}`$ to denote the $`i`$-th standard
basis vector, $`\|\cdot\|_{2}`$ denotes the Euclidean ($`\ell_{2}`$)
norm. $`r^{*}`$ represents real rewards derived from label,
$`r_{\text{covo}}`$ represents the reward function of CoVo.

Overall, our theoretical settings involve two main simplifications.
First, we assume the KL coefficient is relatively small and will not be
dominant. Second, the analysis is based on tabular policies.

#### B.2 Useful Lemmas

###### Lemma 1.

Given a tabular policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ and a prompt
$`x\in\mathcal{X}`$, the following holds:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\nabla\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\theta;x)=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)\cdot r(x,\cdot)-\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,y)].`$ |  | (16) |

###### Proof.

We first compute the gradient of $`\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\theta;x)`$
with respect to the parameter vector $`\theta_{:,x}`$, which corresponds
to the column of parameters for prompt $`x`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nabla\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\theta;x)=\nabla\ \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[r(x,y)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[r(x,y)\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\right].
``` |  | (17) |

Thus, we can write

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\nabla\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\theta;x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\cdot r(x,y)\cdot\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y|x).`$ |  | (18) |

According to the properties of tabular policy \[[39](#bib.bib39)\], we
have
$`\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y|x)=\mathbf{e}_{y}-\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)`$. So
$`\nabla\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\theta;x)`$ can be expressed as:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\nabla\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\theta;x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\cdot r(x,y)\cdot\left(\mathbf{e}_{y}-\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)\right)`$ |  | (19) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\cdot r(x,y)\cdot\mathbf{e}_{y}-\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\cdot r(x,y)\cdot\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)\cdot r(x,\cdot)-\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,y)],`$ |  |  |

which concludes the proof. ∎

###### Lemma 2.

Assuming gradient flow is applied to maximize the RL objective over a
set of prompts $`\mathcal{X}`$. Then, for any prompt
$`x\in\mathcal{X}`$, outputs $`y\subseteq\mathcal{Y}`$, and time
$`T\geq 0`$, such that the following holds:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)^{2}\left[r(x,y)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,y)]\right]`$ |  | (20) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)^{2}\left[r(x,y^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,y)]\right],`$ |  |  |

and

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{\theta(T)}(y|x)\leq\pi_{\theta(0)}(y|x)\cdot\exp\left(2T\right).
``` |  | (21) |

###### Proof.

Since
$`\frac{d}{dt}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)=\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)\cdot\frac{d}{dt}\ln\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)`$,
applying the chain rule and
Lemma [1](#Thmlemma1 "Lemma 1. ‣ B.2 Useful Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning")
we get:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)\cdot\bigl\langle\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x),\frac{d}{dt}\theta(t)\bigr\rangle`$ |  | (22) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)\cdot\bigl\langle\mathbf{e}_{y}-\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x),\nabla\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\theta(t),x)\bigr\rangle`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)\bigl\langle\mathbf{e}_{y}-\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x),\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)\cdot\left[r(x,\cdot)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,y)]\cdot\mathbf{1}\right]\bigr\rangle`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\underbrace{\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)^{2}\left[r(x,y)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,y)]\right]}_{\texttt{(I)}}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-\underbrace{\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)^{2}\left[r(x,y^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,y)]\right]}_{\texttt{(II)}}.`$ |  |  |

Since
$`|r(x,y)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,y)]|\leq 1`$,
the value of (I) + (II) can be bounded as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\texttt{(I)}+\texttt{(II)}\leq\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)^{2}+\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)\leq 2\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x).
``` |  | (23) |

Then we use Grönwall’s inequality and derive:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)\leq\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)\cdot 2\implies\pi_{\theta(T)}(y|x)\leq\pi_{\theta(0)}(y|x)\cdot\exp\left(2T\right).`$ |  | (24) |

Then we complete the proof. ∎

#### B.3 Monotonicity and Robustness of Intrinsic Reward

In
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Self Rewarding in Reinforcement Learning ‣ 3 Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning"),
we propose intrinsic reward formulations $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}`$ and
$`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}`$ that employ two different feature
combination strategies as reward signals. Specifically, the linear
nature of $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}`$ effectively captures the monotonic
characteristics of both the consistency ($`Con(\tau)`$) and volatility
($`Vol(\tau)`$) in a trajectory $`\tau`$. In contrast, the monotonicity
of these two features in $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}`$ is not as
pronounced. Now we formally prove that $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}`$ and
$`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}`$ maintain equivalent monotonic dependencies
on $`Con(\tau)`$ and $`Vol(\tau)`$, while $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}`$
exhibits greater robustness to outliers. Inspired by the incremental
method employed in [Wang et al. \[43\]](#bib.bib43) to establish
monotonicity and robustness, we also adopt this idea for the proof.

We assume $`n`$ reasoning paths in a group, each represented as a pair
of consistency and volatility $`(C_{i},V_{i})`$, where
$`1\leq i\leq n`$. The intrinsic reward for a group is denoted as
$`r_{\text{int}}(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V})`$ with
$`\mathbf{C}=[C_{i}]^{n}_{i=1}`$ and $`\mathbf{V}=[V_{i}]^{n}_{i=1}`$.
Applying increments $`\Delta c`$ to $`C_{i}`$ and $`\Delta v`$ to
$`V_{i}`$, the resulting change in the intrinsic reward is:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta r_{\text{int}}\left(C_{i}\right)=r_{\text{int}}\left(\mathbf{C}+\Delta c\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i},\mathbf{V}\right)-r_{\text{int}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}\right),
``` |  | (25) |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta r_{\text{int}}\left(V_{i}\right)=r_{\text{int}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}+\Delta v\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i}\right)-r_{\text{int}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}\right).
``` |  | (26) |

where $`\mathbf{e}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}`$ denotes the $`i`$-th standard
basis vector with $`i`$-th component being 1 and the others 0.

##### B.3.1 Monotonicity Analysis

For linear intrinsic reward, its group reward can be denoted as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V})=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{C_{i}}{n}-\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{V_{i}}{n},
``` |  | (27) |

Thus, the reward variations with feature increments are:

|     |                                                             |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}(C_{i})=\frac{\Delta c}{n},\\
       \Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}(V_{i})=-\frac{\Delta v}{n},
       ```                                                          |     | (28) |

which ensures $`\Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}(C_{i})>0`$ and
$`\Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}(V_{i})<0`$. That is, higher consistency
and lower volatility indicate a higher $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}`$
reward.

For vector-space intrinsic reward, its group reward can be denoted as:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}C_{j}\cos V_{j}}{n}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}C_{j}\sin V_{j}}{n}\right)^{2}}`$ |  | (29) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sqrt{\sum_{j}C_{j}^{2}+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos V_{k}\cos V_{t}+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t}2C_{k}C_{t}\sin V_{k}\sin V_{t}}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sqrt{\sum_{j}C_{j}^{2}+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos\left(V_{k}-V_{t}\right)}.`$ |  |  |

We denote $`A=\sum_{k,t,k\neq t\neq i}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos(V_{k}-V_{t})`$ and
$`B=\sum_{j,j\neq i}2(C_{i}+\Delta c)C_{j}\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})`$, then the
reward variations with feature increments are:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}(C_{i})=`$ | $`\displaystyle r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C}+\Delta c\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i},\mathbf{V}\right)-r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}\right)`$ |  | (30) |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sqrt{\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}C_{j}^{2}+(C_{i}+\Delta c)^{2}+A+B}\ \ \ \ -`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sqrt{\sum_{j}C_{j}^{2}+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos\left(V_{k}-V_{t}\right)}`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\frac{-C_{i}^{2}+(C_{i}+\Delta c)^{2}+A-\sum_{k,t,k\neq t}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos\left(V_{k}-V_{t}\right)+B)}{n^{2}r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C}+\Delta c\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i},\mathbf{V}\right)+n^{2}r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}\right)}`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\frac{-C_{i}^{2}+(C_{i}+\Delta c)^{2}+\sum_{j,j\neq i}2C_{j}\Delta c\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})}{n^{2}r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C}+\Delta c\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i},\mathbf{V}\right)+n^{2}r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}\right)}`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\frac{\Delta c\left(\Delta c+2C_{i}+2\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})\right)}{n^{2}r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C}+\Delta c\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i},\mathbf{V}\right)+n^{2}r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}\right)},`$ |  |  |

and

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}(V_{i})=`$ | $`\displaystyle r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}+\Delta v\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i}\right)-r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}\right)`$ |  | (31) |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sqrt{\sum_{j}L_{j}^{2}+A+\sum_{j,j\neq i}2C_{i}C_{j}\cos(V_{i}+\Delta v-V_{j})}-`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sqrt{\sum_{j}C_{j}^{2}+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos(V_{k}-V_{t})}`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\frac{A-\sum_{k,t,k\neq t}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos(V_{k}-V_{t})+\sum_{j,j\neq i}2C_{i}C_{j}\cos(V_{i}+\Delta v-V_{j})}{n^{2}r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}+\Delta v\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i}\right)+n^{2}r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}\right)}`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{i,j,i\neq j}2C_{i}C_{j}\left[\cos(V_{i}+\Delta v-V_{j})-\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})\right]}{n^{2}r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}+\Delta v\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i}\right)+n^{2}r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}\right)}`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle\frac{-4\sum_{i,j,i\neq j}C_{i}C_{j}\sin(V_{i}-V_{j}+\frac{\Delta v}{2})\sin(\frac{\Delta v}{2})}{n^{2}r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}+\Delta v\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i}\right)+n^{2}r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}\right)}.`$ |  |  |

In practice, $`V_{i}\in[0,1]`$ guarantees that $`cos(V_{i}-V_{j})>0`$,
which always leads to $`\Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}(C_{i})>0`$. When
$`\Delta v`$ causes $`V_{i}`$ to deviate from the current group, it
tends to be sizable. Therefore $`(V_{i}-V_{j}+\frac{\Delta v}{2})>0`$,
which leads to $`\Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}(V_{i})<0`$. Thus in our
scenario, the monotonicity of $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}`$ on both
magnitude and angle features is consistent with
$`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}`$.

##### B.3.2 Robustness Analysis

In
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Self Rewarding in Reinforcement Learning ‣ 3 Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning"),
we point out that $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}`$ may be more sensitive to
outliers. Empirically, we validate this claim in the ablation study in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning").
Here we provide the theoretical proof.

We already know that correct trajectories tend to exhibit higher
consistency in intermediate reasoning states. Consequently, for a set of
incorrect trajectories, the presence of abnormally large consistency
values in some samples can lead to spurious reward assignments.
Therefore, a reward signal capable of better controlling its increment
under these circumstances would mitigate the risk of incorrect reward
assignments. Therefore, we compare
$`\Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}(C_{i})`$ and
$`\Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}(C_{i})`$ under the same increments
$`\Delta c`$, the smaller one indicates stronger robustness. We denote

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V})=\frac{1}{n}\sqrt{\sum_{j}C_{j}^{2}+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos\left(V_{k}-V_{t}\right)}=\frac{1}{n}\sqrt{S},`$ |  | (32) |

where

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle S`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{j}C_{j}^{2}+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos\left(V_{k}-V_{t}\right)`$ |  | (33) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left(C_{i}+\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})\right)^{2}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}^{2}+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t\neq i}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos(V_{k}-V_{t})-\left(\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})\right)^{2}.`$ |  |  |

Note that

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}^{2}+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t\neq i}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos(V_{k}-V_{t})-\left(\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})\right)^{2}`$ |  | (34) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}^{2}+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t\neq i}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos(V_{k}-V_{t})`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-\left(\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}C_{j}^{2}\cos^{2}(V_{i}-V_{j})+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t\neq i}2C_{k}C_{t}\cos(V_{i}-V_{k})\cos(V_{i}-V_{t})\right)`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}C_{j}^{2}\left[1-\cos^{2}(V_{i}-V_{j})\right]`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t\neq i}2C_{k}C_{t}\left[\cos(V_{k}-V_{t})-\cos(V_{i}-V_{k})\cos(V_{i}-V_{t})\right]`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}C_{j}^{2}\left[1-\cos^{2}(V_{i}-V_{j})\right]`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t\neq i}2C_{k}C_{t}\left[\cos((V_{i}-V_{t})-(V_{i}-V_{k}))-\cos(V_{i}-V_{k})\cos(V_{i}-V_{t})\right]`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}C_{j}^{2}\sin^{2}(V_{i}-V_{j})+\sum_{k,t,k\neq t\neq i}2C_{k}C_{t}\sin(V_{i}-V_{k})\sin(V_{i}-V_{t})`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}C_{j}\sin(V_{i}-V_{j})\right)^{2}.`$ |  |  |

Therfore, we substitute
Eq. ([34](#A2.E34 "In B.3.2 Robustness Analysis ‣ B.3 Monotonicity and Robustness of Intrinsic Reward ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning"))
into
Eq. ([32](#A2.E32 "In B.3.2 Robustness Analysis ‣ B.3 Monotonicity and Robustness of Intrinsic Reward ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning"))
and obtain the following lower bound:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sqrt{\left(C_{i}+\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})\right)^{2}+\left(\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}\sin(V_{i}-V_{j})\right)^{2}}`$ |  | (35) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{n}\left(C_{i}+\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})\right).`$ |  |  |

Then, we use this lower bound to deflate
$`\Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}(C_{i})`$ in
Eq. ([30](#A2.E30 "In B.3.1 Monotonicity Analysis ‣ B.3 Monotonicity and Robustness of Intrinsic Reward ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning")):

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta`$ | $`\displaystyle r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}(C_{i})=\frac{\Delta c\left(\Delta c+2C_{i}+2\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})\right)}{n^{2}\mathcal{R}\left(\mathbf{C}+\Delta c\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i},\mathbf{V}\right)+n^{2}\mathcal{R}\left(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{V}\right)}`$ |  | (36) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\frac{\Delta c\left(\Delta c+2C_{i}+2\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})\right)}{n^{2}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\left(C_{i}+\Delta c+\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})\right)+n^{2}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\left(C_{i}+\sum_{j,j\neq i}C_{j}\cos(V_{i}-V_{j})\right)}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta c}{n}.`$ |  |  |

Note that the right side of
Eq. ([36](#A2.E36 "In B.3.2 Robustness Analysis ‣ B.3 Monotonicity and Robustness of Intrinsic Reward ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning"))
is exactly right side of $`\Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}(C_{i})`$ in
Eq. ([28](#A2.E28 "In B.3.1 Monotonicity Analysis ‣ B.3 Monotonicity and Robustness of Intrinsic Reward ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning")),
which suggests
$`\Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}(C_{i})\leq\Delta r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}(C_{i})`$.
According to the aforementioned analysis, we can conclude that
$`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}`$ is more robust than
$`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}`$ when facing abnormally large outliers.

#### B.4 Proof of Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Model Collapse). ‣ 5.1 Rethinking Majority Voting in RL Optimization ‣ 5 Theoretical Analysis ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning")

###### Proposition 1 (Model Collapse).

Given an input prompt $`x\in\mathcal{X}`$, the policy model sample $`n`$
responses $`\{y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}\}\subseteq\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)`$
and denote $`C(y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}\{y_{i}=y\}.`$ Suppose
$`y^{*}\in\mathcal{Y}`$ that satisfies
$`y^{*}=\operatorname{argmax}_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)`$ and a
reward function $`r:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}`$ defined by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r(x,y)=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }y=\operatorname{argmax}_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}C(y^{\prime}),\\[2.84526pt]
0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (37) |

such that the following hold:

- •
  When using gradient ascent to maximize the RLHF objective with respect
  to the reward function $`r`$, $`\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}\mid x)`$ converges
  to 1 as training proceeds.
- •
  If $`y^{*}`$ is not the ground truth, reward hacking will happen as
  training proceeds.

###### Proof.

We denote the RL object as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{RL}(\theta;x)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[r(x,y)\right],
``` |  | (38) |

By the log-derivative we derive the gradient:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\nabla\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\theta;x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[r(x,y)\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\right]`$ |  | (39) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\cdot r(x,y)\cdot\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y|x).`$ |  |  |

We denote the parameters $`\theta`$ updates from timestep $`t`$ to
$`t+1`$ as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}+\eta\cdot\nabla\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\theta;x)=\theta_{t}+\eta\cdot\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\cdot r(x,y)\cdot\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y|x),
``` |  | (40) |

where $`\eta`$ is the learning rate. According to Taylor’s formula, we
obtain the following equation:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ln\pi_{\theta(t+1)}(y|x)\approx\ln\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)+\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)^{T}\cdot(\theta(t+1)-\theta(t)).
``` |  | (41) |

By substituting
Eq. ([40](#A2.E40 "In Proof. ‣ B.4 Proof of Proposition ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning"))
into
Eq. ([41](#A2.E41 "In Proof. ‣ B.4 Proof of Proposition ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning"))
we can get the log-probability for certain output $`y^{*}`$:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\ln\pi_{\theta(t+1)}(y^{*}|x)`$ | $`\displaystyle\approx\ln\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{*}|x)+\eta\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{*}|x)^{T}\cdot\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)r(x,y)\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y|x)`$ |  | (42) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\ln\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{*}|x)+\eta\bigg(\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x)r(x,y^{*})\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x)\cdot\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x)^{T}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\sum_{y,y\neq y^{*}}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)r(x,y)\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\cdot\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x)^{T}\bigg)`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\ln\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{*}|x)+\eta\bigg(\underbrace{\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x)r(x,y^{*})\|\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x)\|_{2}^{2}}_{\texttt{(I)}}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\underbrace{\sum_{y,y\neq y^{*}}\pi_{\theta}(y|x)r(x,y)\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\cdot\nabla\ln\pi_{\theta}(y^{*}|x)^{T}}_{\texttt{(II)}}\bigg)`$ |  |  |

In our setup, $`y^{*}`$ is defined as the response that has the highest
count $`C(y)`$ among the $`n`$ sampled responses, which means
$`r(x,y^{*})=1`$ and $`r(x,y)=0`$ for $`y\neq y^{*}`$. Therefore, term
(I) is non-negative and term (II) is 0, which indicates the value of
(I) + (II) is larger than 0.

Since $`\pi(y^{*}\mid x)\leq 1`$, we have
$`\ln\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{*}\mid x)\;\leq\;\ln 1=0`$. Thus the sequence
$`\{\ln\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{*}\mid x)\}_{t=0}^{\infty}`$ is monotonically
increasing and bounded above by $`0`$. By the Monotone Convergence
Theorem, $`\{\ln\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{*}\mid x)\}`$ will converge to its
upper bound 0:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\lim_{t\to\infty}\ln\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{*}\mid x)\;=\;0\quad\implies\quad\lim_{t\to\infty}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{*}\mid x)\;=\;1.
``` |  | (43) |

To conclude, if $`y^{*}`$ is not the “ground-truth” desired output but
merely the sample-mode that maximizes $`C(y)`$, the above shows that the
policy will collapse to always output $`y^{*}`$, regardless of whether
it semantically or factually answers the prompt correctly. In other
words, the model has “hacked” the reward by finding a high-frequency
sample that maximizes rewards $`r`$, rather than by producing the true
correct response. ∎

#### B.5 Proof of Proposition [2](#Thmproposition2 "Proposition 2 (Variational Optimization for Reasoning). ‣ 5.2 Theoretical Foundations of Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning ‣ 5 Theoretical Analysis ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning")

We aim to establish a variational lower bound for the conditional
likelihood $`\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)`$, by introducing a latent variable
$`s`$ representing latent reasoning paths. The idea is to show that
optimizing this lower bound corresponds to assigning rewards to
consistent reasoning paths, enabling the model to learn not only answer
generation but also the intermediate states leading to those answers.

###### Proposition 2 (Variational Optimization for Reasoning).

Let $`\pi_{\theta}(y|x)`$ denote a language model that generates final
answers $`y`$ conditioned on input prompt $`x`$, with $`s`$ representing
latent intermediate reasoning states. Suppose the reasoning state is
guided by a prior distribution $`\pi_{\theta(0)}(s|x)`$ and define the
reward function
$`r(s,x,y)\in[0,1]\propto\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x\oplus s)`$, the following
optimizing bound holds:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\geq\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{s,y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[r(s,y,x)\right]}_{\text{Reward Assignment}}-\underbrace{D_{\text{KL}}\left[\pi_{\theta}(s|x)\,\|\,\pi_{\theta(0)}(s|x)\right]}_{\text{KL Regularization}},
``` |  | (44) |

where $`\oplus`$ denotes the concatenation of the input prompt $`x`$
with the reasoning state $`s`$.

###### Proof.

We first introduce the latent variable $`s`$ as latent reasoning states.
We begin by expressing the marginal likelihood of the output $`y`$
conditioned on input $`x`$ by marginalizing over reasoning states $`s`$
with respect to a prior distribution $`\pi_{\theta(0)}(s|x)`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)=\log\int\pi_{\theta}(y|x,s)\pi_{\theta(0)}(s|x)\ ds,
``` |  | (45) |

where $`\pi_{\theta}(y|x,s)`$ denotes the probability of generating
output $`y`$ given input $`x`$ augmented with the intermediate reasoning
states $`s`$, i.e., $`\pi_{\theta}(y|x,s):=\pi_{\theta}(y|x\oplus s)`$.

After that, we introduce a variational distribution
$`\pi_{\theta}(s|x)`$ over the latent states and rewrite the integral
using importance sampling:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\log\int\frac{\pi_{\theta}(s|x)}{\pi_{\theta}(s|x)}\pi_{\theta}(y|x,s)\pi_{\theta(0)}(s|x)\,ds`$ |  | (46) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\log\mathbb{E}_{s,y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y|x,s)\pi_{\theta(0)}(s|x)}{\pi_{\theta}(s|x)}\right].`$ |  |  |

Applying Jensen’s inequality yields the evidence lower bound (ELBO):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\geq\mathbb{E}_{s,y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x,s)+\log\pi_{\theta(0)}(s|x)-\log\pi_{\theta}(s|x)\right],
``` |  | (47) |

which simplifies to:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\geq\mathbb{E}_{s,y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x\oplus s)\right]-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left[\pi_{\theta}(s|x)\|\pi_{\theta(0)}(s|x)\right].
``` |  | (48) |

Recall that the reward function is defined as:
$`r(s,x,y)\propto\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x\oplus s)`$. Without affecting the
optimization, $`\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x\oplus s)`$ can be directly regarded
as part of the reward function (since the constant ratio will not affect
the final learning goal), then the above bound yields:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\log\pi_{\theta}(y|x)\geq\mathbb{E}_{s,y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[r(s,x,y)\right]-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left[\pi_{\theta}(s|x)\|\pi_{\theta(0)}(s|x)\right],
``` |  | (49) |

which completes the derivation. This formulation shows that optimizing
the output likelihood can be interpreted as assigning rewards to latent
reasoning states while regularizing their distribution toward a prior.
Hence, self-rewarding reinforcement learning corresponds to performing
approximate variational inference over reasoning trajectories, thereby
coupling answer generation and reasoning trajectory inference in a
principled manner. ∎

#### B.6 Proof of Proposition [3](#Thmproposition3 "Proposition 3 (Convergence). ‣ 5.3 Complexity and Convergence of CoVo ‣ 5 Theoretical Analysis ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning")

To analyze the convergence of CoVo, we establish the following
proposition. The core idea of this proof is adapted from [Razin et al.
\[32\]](#bib.bib32), with simplifications tailored to the context of our
work.

###### Proposition 3 (Convergence).

Let $`\mathcal{X}`$ denote prompt sets, and $`\gamma>0`$ represent the
expected increase of real reward $`r^{*}`$. For a prompt
$`x\in\mathcal{X}`$, let $`y^{\gamma}`$ denote the final answer in a
reasoning trajectory with higher consistency and lower volatility.
Define $`T^{\prime}`$ as the initial time where
$`\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[r^{*}(x,y)\right]\geq\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}\left[r^{*}(x,y)\right]+\gamma`$.
We assume the following conditions hold:

- •
  Our reward function ranks $`y^{\gamma}`$ highest among all candidates;
- •
  Our reward function has a low probability of misclassifying incorrect
  trajectories;
- •
  The KL regularization coefficient is sufficiently small.

Then the convergence time for achieving the expected increase in real
reward satisfies the upper bound
$`T^{\prime}\leq\mathcal{O}(\pi_{\theta(0)}(y^{\gamma}|x)^{-1})`$.

###### Proof.

We first formalize these assumptions. Define
$`\mathcal{Y}^{+}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}`$ be a set of outputs such that
each $`y^{\gamma}\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}`$ s.t.
$`r^{*}(x,y^{\gamma})>\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}[r^{*}(x,y)]+\gamma`$
and
$`r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\gamma})>\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]`$,
$`\mathcal{Y}^{-}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}`$ be a set of outputs s.t.
$`\mathcal{Y^{-}}=\{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}\mid r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})>\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]\}\backslash\mathcal{Y^{+}}`$.
Assume that the initial probability of $`\mathcal{Y}^{-}`$ is small:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{\theta(0)}(\mathcal{Y}^{-}|x)\leq\frac{\sigma(1-\rho)\pi_{\theta(0)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)^{2}}{4|\mathcal{Y}^{+}|}\exp\left(-2T^{\prime}\right),
``` |  | (50) |

where
$`\rho=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}\left[r^{*}(x,y)\right]+\gamma\in[0,1]`$
and
$`\sigma=(1-\rho)(\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}}r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)])=(1-\rho)(1-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)])`$.

Since

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}\left[r^{*}(x,y)\right]`$ | $`\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)\cdot 1-(1-\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x))\cdot 0`$ |  | (51) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\rho=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}\left[r^{*}(x,y)\right]+\gamma,`$ |  |  |

we can find that $`\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)\geq\rho`$ implies
$`\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}\left[r^{*}(x,y)\right]\geq\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}\left[r^{*}(x,y)\right]+\gamma`$.
Thus, it suffices to show that $`\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)`$
reaches $`\rho`$ within a finite time $`T^{\prime}`$.

For $`t\in[0,T^{\prime})`$ and $`y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}`$, by
Lemma [2](#Thmlemma2 "Lemma 2. ‣ B.2 Useful Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning")
we know:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)^{2}\left[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]\right]`$ |  | (52) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)^{2}\left[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]\right].`$ |  |  |

Summing all outputs in $`\mathcal{Y}^{+}`$ then derives the following:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{y^{\gamma}\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)^{2}\left[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\gamma})-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]\right]`$ |  | (53) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)^{2}\left[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]\right]`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=(1-\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x))\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)^{2}\underbrace{\left[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]\right]}_{\texttt{(A)}}`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}\backslash\mathcal{Y}^{+}}\underbrace{\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)^{2}\left[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]\right]}_{\texttt{(B)}}.`$ |  |  |

To derive the lower bound of $`\frac{d}{dt}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)`$, we
begin to analyze the terms $`A`$ and $`B`$ above.

First, the value of term $`A`$ is:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle A`$ | $`\displaystyle=r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]`$ |  | (54) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)-\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)\ r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)\left(r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})\right)`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}\backslash\mathcal{Y}^{+}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)\left(r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})\right).`$ |  |  |

Through the definitions of $`\mathcal{Y}^{+}`$ and $`\mathcal{Y}^{-}`$,
for any
$`y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}\backslash(\mathcal{Y}^{+}\cup\mathcal{Y}^{-})`$,
we know that
$`r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})\leq\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}\left[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)\right]`$,
which impiles
$`r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})\geq r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}\left[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)\right]`$.
Thus we can derive the following inequality:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle A`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}\setminus\mathcal{Y}^{+}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)(r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime}))`$ |  | (55) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}^{-}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)(r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime}))`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}\setminus(\mathcal{Y}^{+}\cup\mathcal{Y}^{-})}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)(r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime}))`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}^{-}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)(r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime}))`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}\setminus(\mathcal{Y}^{+}\cup\mathcal{Y}^{-})}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)(r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}\left[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)\right])`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}^{-}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)(\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]-r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime}))`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+(1-\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x))(r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]).`$ |  |  |

Since we assume that $`\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)`$ reaches
$`\rho`$ at timestep $`T^{\prime}`$,
$`\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)<\rho`$ for $`t\in[0,T^{\prime})`$.
We also have
$`|\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]-r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})|\leq 1`$
for $`y\in\mathcal{Y}`$, we obtain:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle A`$ | $`\displaystyle\geq(1-\rho)(r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(0)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)])-\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{-}|x)`$ |  | (56) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sigma-\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{-}|x).`$ |  |  |

Second, the value of term $`B`$ is:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle B`$ | $`\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)^{2}\left[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]\right]`$ |  | (57) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)^{2}\sum_{y\notin\mathcal{Y}^{-}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)(r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})-r_{\text{covo}}(x,y))`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)^{2}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{-}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)(r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})-r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)).`$ |  |  |

According to the definition of $`\mathcal{Y}^{-}`$, we have
$`r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})-r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)=0`$ for any
$`y\notin\mathcal{Y}^{-}`$ and
$`r_{\text{covo}}(x,y^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta(t)}(\cdot|x)}[r_{\text{covo}}(x,y)]\leq 1`$
for $`y\in\mathcal{Y}^{-}`$, the above equation leads to:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
B\leq\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x)^{2}\leq\pi_{\theta(t)}(y^{\prime}|x).
``` |  | (58) |

By deriving the lower bound and upper bound of terms $`A`$ and $`B`$
respectively, we obtain the lower bound of
Eq. ([53](#A2.E53 "In Proof. ‣ B.6 Proof of Proposition ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning")):

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)`$ | $`\displaystyle\geq(1-\rho)\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}^{+}}\pi_{\theta(t)}(y|x)^{2}(\sigma-\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{-}|x))-\rho\cdot\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{-}|x)`$ |  | (59) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\geq\frac{(1-\rho)}{|\mathcal{Y}^{+}|}(\sigma-\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{-}|x))\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)^{2}-\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{-}|x).`$ |  |  |

From
Lemma [2](#Thmlemma2 "Lemma 2. ‣ B.2 Useful Lemmas ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning"),
we know that

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{-}|x)\leq\pi_{\theta(0)}(\mathcal{Y}^{-}|x)\cdot\exp\left(2T^{\prime}\right)=\frac{\sigma(1-\rho)\pi_{\theta(0)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)^{2}}{4|\mathcal{Y}^{+}|}\leq\frac{\sigma}{4}\leq\frac{\sigma}{2}.`$ |  | (60) |

Substituting the above inequality into
Eq. ([59](#A2.E59 "In Proof. ‣ B.6 Proof of Proposition ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning")),
we obtain:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{d}{dt}\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)\geq\frac{(1-\rho)\sigma}{4|\mathcal{Y}^{+}|}\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)^{2}.
``` |  | (61) |

Denote $`\pi(t)=\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}\mid x)`$, we can rewrite
Eq. ([61](#A2.E61 "In Proof. ‣ B.6 Proof of Proposition ‣ Appendix B Proof and Analysis ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning"))
as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{\mathrm{d}\pi(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}\geq\frac{(1-\rho)\sigma}{4|\mathcal{Y}^{+}|}\ \pi(t)^{2}.
``` |  | (62) |

We divide both sides of the equation by $`\pi(t)^{2}`$ and get:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{1}{\pi(t)^{2}}\frac{d\pi(t)}{dt}\geq\frac{(1-\rho)\sigma}{4|\mathcal{Y}^{+}|}\quad\implies\quad\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{1}{\pi(t)}\right)\geq\frac{(1-\rho)\sigma}{4|\mathcal{Y}^{+}|}.
``` |  | (63) |

Next, we integrate both sides of the inequality. Assume that $`\pi(t)`$
evolves from its initial value $`\pi(0)`$ at time $`t=0`$ to the value
$`\rho`$ at some time $`t=T^{\prime}`$. The integration becomes:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\int_{0}^{T^{\prime}}\frac{d}{dt}\!\bigl[\pi(t)^{-1}\bigr]\ dt\geq\int_{0}^{T^{\prime}}\frac{(1-\rho)\sigma}{4|\mathcal{Y}^{+}|}\ dt.
``` |  | (64) |

Substituting the results of both integrals into the inequality, we get:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{1}{\pi(0)}-\frac{1}{\rho}\geq\frac{(1-\rho)\sigma}{4|\mathcal{Y}^{+}|}T^{\prime}.
``` |  | (65) |

Finally, solving for $`T^{\prime}`$ we obtain:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
T^{\prime}\leq\frac{4|\mathcal{Y}^{+}|}{(1-\rho)\sigma}\left(\frac{1}{\pi(0)}-\frac{1}{\rho}\right)=\frac{4|\mathcal{Y}^{+}|}{(1-\rho)\sigma}\left(\frac{1}{\pi_{\theta(0)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)}-\frac{1}{\rho}\right)=\mathcal{O}(\pi_{0}(y^{\gamma}|x)^{-1}).
``` |  | (66) |

This inequality indicates that when $`t=T^{\prime}`$,
$`\pi_{\theta(t)}(\mathcal{Y}^{+}|x)\geq\rho`$, which means the increase
by $`\gamma`$ of the real reward. Then we complete the proof. ∎

### Appendix C Algorithm: Reward Computation

To facilitate reproducibility, we provide the detailed algorithm for
computing intrinsic reward and curiosity reward in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix C Algorithm: Reward Computation ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning")
and
Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix C Algorithm: Reward Computation ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning"),
respectively.

0:  $`G`$: The number of trajectories in a group with the same answer
$`\bm{D_{1}},\bm{D_{2}},...,\bm{D_{G}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times K}`$:
Distance Matrix of all trajectories

1:  $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}`$ $`\leftarrow 0`$

2:  for $`i\leftarrow 0`$ to $`G-1`$ do

3:   $`\mathrm{Con}\leftarrow 0`$

4:   $`\mathrm{Vol}\leftarrow 0`$

5:   $`\bm{V_{G}}\leftarrow\bm{0}`$

6:   for $`t\leftarrow 0`$ to $`T-1`$ do

7:    if $`\bm{D}[t,0]==\min\bm{D}[t,:]`$ then

8:     $`\mathrm{Con}\leftarrow\mathrm{Con}+1/T`$

9:    else

10:     $`\mathrm{Vol}\leftarrow t/T`$

11:    end if

12:   end for

13:   $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}`$ $`\leftarrow`$
$`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}`$ + $`\mathrm{Con}-\mathrm{Vol}`$

14:
  $`\bm{V_{G}}\leftarrow\bm{V_{G}}+[\mathrm{Con}\cdot\cos(\mathrm{Vol}),\mathrm{Con}\cdot\sin(\mathrm{Vol})]`$

15:  end for

16:  $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}`$
$`\leftarrow r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}/G`$

17:  $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{L}}`$, $`r_{\text{int}}^{\bm{V}}`$

Algorithm 1 Intrinsic Reward Computation

0:  $`T`$: The number of intermediate reasoning states in a trajectory
$`s_{1},s_{2},...,s_{T}`$: All intermediate reasoning states

1:  $`r_{\text{cur}}`$ $`\leftarrow 0`$

2:  for $`i\leftarrow 0`$ to $`T-1`$ do

3:   $`\mathrm{Distance}\leftarrow 0`$

4:   $`\mathcal{P}=[]`$

5:   for $`t\leftarrow\mathrm{len}(s_{i})`$ to $`\mathrm{len}(s_{i+1})`$
do

6:    $`\mathrm{logprob}=\log\pi_{\theta}(s_{i+1}[t]|s_{i+1}[:t])`$

7:    $`\mathrm{Distance}\leftarrow\mathrm{Distance}+\mathrm{logprob}`$

8:    $`\mathcal{P}.\mathrm{append(\mathrm{logprob})}`$

9:   end for

10:
  $`\mathrm{Distance}\leftarrow\mathrm{Distance}/(\mathrm{len}(s_{i+1})-\mathrm{len}(s_{i}))`$

11:
  $`\mathrm{KLP}=\ln[\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{\mathcal{P},\mathcal{U}})+1]`$

12:
  $`r_{\text{cur}}\leftarrow r_{\text{cur}}+\mathrm{Distance}-\mathrm{KLP}`$

13:  end for

14:  $`r_{\text{cur}}`$ $`\leftarrow r_{\text{cur}}/T`$

14:  $`r_{\text{cur}}`$

### Appendix D Datasets Details

We select six datasets in three different domains for evaluation in our
experiments, and list details about our evaluation datasets in
Table [8](#A4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ D.2 Evaluation ‣ Appendix D Datasets Details ‣ Appendix ‣ Consistent Paths Lead to Truth: Self-Rewarding Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning").
We briefly describe the information of each dataset.

#### D.1 Training

The training dataset of Open-Reasoner-Zero \[[15](#bib.bib15)\]
comprises public data from various sources, including AIME (up to 2023),
MATH \[[12](#bib.bib12)\], Numina-Math collection \[[20](#bib.bib20)\],
Tulu3 MATH \[[19](#bib.bib19)\], OpenR1-Math-220k \[[2](#bib.bib2)\] and
other opensource datasets. It also includes additional synthesized
reasoning tasks using programmatic approaches to augment the dataset.

#### D.2 Evaluation

- •
  Mathematical Domain: MATH-500 \[[22](#bib.bib22)\] dataset contains
  500 high school–level math problems, covering 7 major areas such as
  precalculus, algebra, and number theory. GSM8K \[[7](#bib.bib7)\]
  contains 1318 elementary school math problems, each requiring 2 to 8
  steps to solve and mainly involving basic arithmetic operations. The
  AMC–23³³ 3 https://huggingface.co/datasets/AI-MO/aimo-validation-amc
  dataset contains 40 high school–level math competition problems, which
  are challenging and diverse in form. Olympiad
  Bench \[[11](#bib.bib11)\] includes challenging math problems sourced
  from international Olympiads, Chinese Olympiads, and the Chinese
  College Entrance Examination.
- •
  Commonsense Domain: MMLU-Pro \[[45](#bib.bib45)\] covers a wide range
  of fields, including natural sciences, social sciences, humanities,
  and some interdisciplinary content, which can effectively assess both
  the knowledge base and reasoning abilities of LLMs.
  CommonsenseQA \[[40](#bib.bib40)\] mainly includes a series of
  commonsense questions involving various aspects such as daily life,
  social culture, and natural phenomena, which aim to assess LLM’s
  understanding of commonsense knowledge.
- •
  Science Domain: GPQA \[[34](#bib.bib34)\] is a multiple-choice, Q&A
  dataset of very hard questions written and validated by experts in
  biology, physics, and chemistry, which measures LLM’s knowledge and
  reasoning capabilities in scientific fields.

### Appendix F Broader Impact

Our work introduces CoVo, a novel self-rewarding reinforcement learning
framework that enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to improve their
reasoning capabilities without relying on human-annotated labels or
pretrained reward models. It has the potential to enhance reasoning
quality in scenarios with limited labels, such as scientific education,
programming, healthcare, and beyond. The intrinsic reward mechanism also
encourages models to develop more coherent and logically grounded
reasoning processes, which may contribute to improved model
interpretability and robustness.
````
